parole.significato: a trajectory, a course, a path (path that something moves along, especially in physics, astronomy, or the like)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bāne, from Old Saxon *bana, from Proto-West Germanic *banu, from Proto-Germanic *banō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-.

From Old Swedish bedragha, from Middle Low German bedregen, from Old Saxon bidriogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan. By surface analysis, be- + draga, etymologically equivalent to be- + dryga. Displaced native svika in this sense.
Borrowed from Middle Low German begripen, from Old Saxon bigrīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrīpan. Equivalent to be- + gripa.
Old Swedish behof, borrowed from Middle Low German behof, from Old Saxon *bihōf, from Proto-West Germanic *bihōf.

parole.significato: seal (affix a seal in order to prove authenticity or attest to accuracy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish besighla, from Middle Low German besigelen, from Old Saxon *bisiglian, from Proto-West Germanic *bisigilōn. Cognate of Danish besegle, Dutch bezegelen, German besiegeln. Related to försegla, insegel, sigill.
From Middle Low German besetten, from Old Saxon *bisettian, from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Proto-Germanic *bisatjaną (“to beset”), equivalent to be- + sätta.
From Old Swedish bethækkia, from Middle Low German bedecken, from Old Saxon *bithekkian, from Proto-West Germanic *biþakkjan, equivalent to be- + täcka.

parole.significato: cheap; of low price, of little worth
parole.testo: From Middle Low German billik, billich, from Proto-West Germanic *bilalīk. Compare German billig and Dutch billijk.
From Middle Low German blank, from Old Saxon blank, from Proto-West Germanic *blank. Displaced native Swedish black, from Old Norse blakkr.

Apocopic form of bliva, from Old Swedish bliva, from Middle Low German blîven (“to remain”), from Old Saxon bilīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *bilīban, from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną. Displaced Swedish varda completely in the present tense, and partly in the past tense.

parole.significato: a block, a boulder, a cuboid (of ice, wood, rock)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German block, from Old Saxon blok, from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką.
From Old Swedish bokka, bukka, from Middle Low German bucken, from Old Saxon *bukkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bukkōn.

parole.significato: to wax or polish a floor
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bônen, from Old Saxon *bōnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bōnōn. Cognate with Dutch boenen, German bohnern.

parole.significato: to use to (present tense of used to); to be in the habit of
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bruken, from Old Saxon brukan.

parole.significato: to make a deep, humming or growling sound (of for example a bear, an engine, or a fan)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brummen, from Old Saxon *brummōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brummōn.

parole.significato: to argue, to fight, to brawl, to make trouble
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brake, probably from or related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan. Compare Middle Dutch braak.

From Middle Low German büken, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *bōkijā (“beech”). Related to German bauchen and German bäuchen. Cognate of French buer and English buck (“to soak, steep or boil in lye or suds”).

From Old Swedish bæver, from Middle Low German biber, bever, from Old Saxon biƀar, biƀor, from Proto-West Germanic *bebru, from Proto-Germanic *bebruz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus. Displaced native bjur.
From Middle Low German bodel, from Old Saxon budil, from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“bailiff, one who carries out an order”).

Inherited from Old Swedish delaktogher, from Middle Low German delhaftich, delachtich, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *daili (“part, share”) + *haft (“captive”). Cognate of Danish delagtig, archaic Dutch deelachtich, German teilhaftig.
From Old Swedish doch, dogh, dog, thoch, thok, tog, from Middle Low German doch, from Old Saxon thōh‚ from Proto-West Germanic *þauh. Replaced native Old Swedish þo, from Old Norse þó.
From Middle Low German dolk, from Old Saxon *dalk, from Proto-West Germanic *dalk, from Proto-Germanic *dalkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰalg-, *dʰalk-.
From Middle Low German dōpe, from Old Saxon dōpi, from Proto-West Germanic *daupīni, from Proto-Germanic *daupīniz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. Doublet of doppa and djup.

From Middle Low German düppen, from Old Saxon dopian, from Proto-West Germanic *daupijan, from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną, to dip (in a liquid), to immerse. See there for further descendants. Doublet of dop, döpa, and djup.

parole.significato: to throw (form clay into objects with the help of a potter's wheel)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German dreien, from Old Saxon thrāian, from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną.
Borrowed from Middle Low German drîstich, from drîste + -ich, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī. By surface analysis, drista + -ig.
From Middle Low German drūve (“bunch”), from Old Saxon thrūvo, from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō (compare German Traube (“bunch, grape”)), from Old High German drūbo).

parole.significato: good; talented; capable (showing good ability, in a sense that includes both being good at something and being well-beh…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German duchtich, from Old Saxon *duhtig, from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg (“strong, proficient”). Parallel borrowing with Danish dygtig, Norwegian dyktig.
From Middle Low German dūken *ducken, from Old Saxon *dūkan *dukkan, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan.

parole.significato: drowsy (in a relaxed manner, for example after lying out in the sun)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German dosich, from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg. Cognate of English dizzy. By surface analysis, dåsa + -ig (“-y”).
From Old Swedish ælænde, answering to Danish elende; from Middle Low German elende, ellende, from Proto-West Germanic *alljas (“other”) + *land (“land”).
From Old Swedish falsker, borrowed from Middle Low German valsch, from Old Saxon *falski, from Proto-West Germanic *falskī (“false, counterfeit”).

parole.significato: to grasp, take (hold in one's hand); the concrete meaning of grasp
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vāten, from Old Saxon *fatōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną. Cognate with Danish fatte, Norwegian Bokmål fatte, Dutch vatten and German fassen.

Inherited from Old Swedish feghþ, feyd, borrowed from Middle Low German veide, from Old Saxon *fēhitha, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“enmity, feud”). Cognate of Old High German fēhida, German Fehde, Old English fǣhð.
From Middle Low German vīle, from Old Saxon fila, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō. Cognate with English file and German Feile.
From Middle Low German vinke, from Old Saxon *fink, from Proto-Germanic *finkiz.

parole.significato: a thin sharp piece of wood or rock or some other material that splinters easily; a splinter, a chip (of rock)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vlise, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *flint. Cognate with German Fliese, Old Norse flís.

From Old Swedish flit, from Middle Low German vlīt, vlît, from Old Saxon *flīt, from Proto-West Germanic *flīt, from Proto-Germanic *flītaz, for which compare *flītan (“to strive”). See also German Low German Fliet, Saterland Frisian Fliet, Dutch vlijt, Danish flid, Norwegian Bokmål flid, Norwegian
From Middle Low German vri, from Old Saxon frī, from Proto-West Germanic *frī, from Proto-Germanic *frijaz.

From Old Swedish frisker, from Middle Low German vrisch, from Old Saxon *frisk, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-. Doublet of fresk, fräsch, and färsk.

parole.significato: to fear, to dread, to be afraid
parole.testo: From Old Swedish frukta, frokta, frykta, from Middle Low German vruchten, from Old Saxon forhtian, from Proto-West Germanic *furhtijan.
From Middle Low German vrāge (German Frage), from Proto-West Germanic *frāgu, from Proto-Germanic *frēgō. Compare English frain. Displaced native spörja (“to ask”), spörsmål (“question”).

parole.significato: Miss ((title for an) unmarried woman (of any class – see usage notes below))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish fröken, from Middle Low German vröuken, vrouwicken, diminutive of vrûwe, vrouwe (“woman, lady”), from Old Saxon frūa, from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjā.
From Middle Low German vuchtich (“moist”), derived from vucht (“moist, moisture”), from Old Saxon *fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht.

Old Swedish fulbordha, from Middle Low German vulborden, based on the noun vulbort (“full board, a ship built to completion”), from Old Saxon ful + bord which is from Proto-West Germanic *bord. The Old Swedish fulbordha was both a verb and adjective, still used as an adjective in the 1526 Bible tran
From Old Swedish fækta, from Middle Low German vechten, from Old Saxon fehtan, from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan, from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną. Compare Dutch vechten and English fight.

parole.significato: a field, a (physical) area, an open space in a landscape (for farming or battle)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fält, from Middle Low German velt, from Old Saxon feld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, cognate with Old English feld, English field, also related to fjäll.
From Middle Low German voracht, from Old Saxon, from Proto-West Germanic *firiahtu, from *firi- (“across, through”) + *ahtu (“attention, consideration”). Cognate with German Verachtung.

From Old Swedish fordriva, from Middle Low German vordriven, from Old Saxon fardrīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *fradrīban, equivalent to för- + driva. Cognate with Danish fordrive, Norwegian Bokmål fordrive, Norwegian Nynorsk fordriva, fordrive, Old Norse fordrífa, German vertreiben and English for
Borrowed from Middle Low German vörvelschen, vorvelschen, from Old Saxon *farfalskōn, from Proto-West Germanic *frafalskōn. By surface analysis, för- + falsk + -a. Cognate of Danish forfalske.

parole.significato: to forget; to lose remembrance of
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forgæta, from Middle Low German vorgēten, from Old Saxon fargetan, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan.

parole.significato: to be wrecked, to go under, to sink (of a ship)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorlisen, vorlêsen (“to lose”), from Old Saxon farliosan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraleusan, from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną. Doublet of förlora (“to lose”). Compare Danish forlise, Norwegian forlise, Dutch verliezen, German verlieren, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍃𐌰𐌽 (fraliusan).

parole.significato: to lose (a competition, fight, or the like)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorloren (German verloren), the past participle of vorlêsen (“to lose”), from Old Saxon farliosan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraleusan, from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną. Doublet of förlisa. Compare Afrikaans verloor.
From Middle Low German gaffel, gaffele, from Old Saxon gavala, gafila, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu, possibly from Celtic.
From Middle Low German gerwen, from Old Saxon gerwian, from Proto-West Germanic *garwijan, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk garva (“tan”) and Danish garve (“tan”). (laugh)
Borrowed from Middle Low German gelik, from Old Saxon gilīk, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.

Borrowed from Middle Low German gemēn, from Old Saxon gimeni, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz. Cognate with English mean, German gemein, Dutch gemeen, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (gamains) and Latin communis.

parole.significato: to move smoothly along a surface; to slide, to slip, to glide, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German glīden, from Old Saxon glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleydʰ-.
From Middle Low German grēve, from Old Saxon grāvio, from Proto-West Germanic *garāfijō. Cognate to Danish greve and English reeve.
From Middle Low German krōde, krode, from Old Saxon *kroda, from Proto-West Germanic *krodu (“toad”) of origin unknown, related to German Kröte. Compare dialectal Norwegian Nynorsk gro (“toad”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German *groll, grull (“grudge”), from Old Saxon *grullio, from Proto-West Germanic *grulljō.

parole.significato: stove, heater; an enclosed space in which fuel (usually wood) is burned to provide heating, usually for cooking
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hærþer, from Middle Low German herd, from Old Saxon heorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ.

parole.significato: to mock, deride, make fun of
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hônen, from Old Saxon hōnian, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan (“to humiliate”). Compare Danish håne.

parole.significato: to hurry, to speed (move quickly and hurriedly)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ila, from Middle Low German īlen, from Proto-West Germanic *īlijan (“to make haste, hasten”).

From Middle Low German īwer, possibly originally from Proto-West Germanic *aibr, from Proto-Germanic *aibraz (“sharp, bitter, vehement, dire, violent”, adj.). Cognate with Danish iver, Norwegian Bokmål iver, Norwegian Nynorsk iver, German Eifer, Luxembourgish Äifer, Dutch ijver and Afrikaans ywer.

parole.significato: to do pelvic thrusts (during sex or otherwise), to hump
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German jücken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *jukkjan.

parole.significato: a hinged flap able to be raised and lowered
parole.testo: Probably related to klapp, itself borrowed from Middle Low German klap, from Old Saxon klappōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn (“to strike, clap, make a loud sound”).

parole.significato: to complain (whether in a whiny way or not)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klagha, borrowed from Middle Low German klagen, from Old Saxon klagon, from Proto-West Germanic *klagōn (“to lament, complain”).

parole.significato: a cliff, a rock (a cliff, or a rock formation with a cliff or cliffs (a steep rock formation, put differently) – compar…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German klippe, related to klif (“cliff, rock”), from Old Saxon *klif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.
From Old Swedish klēver, from Middle Low German klêver, via Old Saxon from Proto-West Germanic *klaibrā. Cognate of Danish kløver, English clover. In sense 2, semantic loan from French trèfle.

parole.significato: a (foot) soldier (especially in the medieval and early modern period)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German knecht, from Old Saxon kneht, from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.

parole.significato: a chef, a cook (person who prepares food for a living)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kok, kock, from Old Saxon kok, from Proto-West Germanic *kok, from Latin coquus.

parole.significato: to boil (turn from liquid into gas by creating gas bubbles throughout the liquid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kôken, from Old Saxon *kokōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn.
From Middle Low German kort, from Old Saxon *kurt, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, an early borrowing from Latin curtus. Cognate with German kurz, Dutch kort, Danish kort and Norwegian Bokmål kort.
From Middle Low German kran, from krane (“crane”), from Old Saxon *krano, from Proto-West Germanic *kranō.
Inherited from Old Swedish krasse, from Middle Low German karse, from Proto-West Germanic *krassjā. Cognate with German Kresse, French cresson.

parole.significato: a pot (container, often made of clay, for example for growing a plant in (blomkruka))
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle Low German krûke, from Old Saxon krūka, from Proto-West Germanic *krūkā (“pot, pitcher”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics ar
From Middle Low German krum, from Old Saxon krumb, from Proto-West Germanic *krump, from Proto-Germanic *krumpaz.

Borrowed and clipped from Middle Low German büssenkrūt, bussenkrût (“gunpowder”), from büsse (“rifle”) + krût (“spice, herb”), from Old Saxon krūd, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“herb, plant”). Doublet of krydda.

parole.significato: a crutch (device to assist in motion)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krykkia, from Middle Low German krucke, krocke, krücke, from Old Saxon krukka, from Proto-West Germanic *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (whence also English crutch), from Proto-Indo-European *grewg-.

parole.significato: to attack or violate someone's personal honor (with words or actions); to violate, to disrespect, to insult, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krænkia, from Middle Low German krenken, from Old Saxon *krenkian, from Proto-West Germanic *krankijan. Cognate of German kränken, Dutch krenken, Danish krænke, Norwegian krenke, Icelandic krenkja.

From Old Swedish kæke, probably borrowed from Middle Low German kêke, from Old Saxon *kioka, from Proto-West Germanic *keukā. Cognate with Danish kiæge, Norwegian kjake, English choke, cheek (from Old English ċēoce (“jaw”)).

Inherited from Old Swedish kæmpe, from Middle Low German kempe, from Old Saxon kempio, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“battlefield”). Cognate of Norwegian kjempe, Danish kæmpe, German Kämpe. Compare English champion.

parole.significato: a goahti (traditional dwelling of the Sami people)
parole.testo: From a confluence of: # Middle Low German kāte, kōte (“hut”), from Old Saxon *kota, from Proto-West Germanic *kotā, from Proto-Germanic *kutǭ ~ *kutą (“stall, tent”); compare German Kate. # A derivative of Proto-Samic *koatē, from Proto-Uralic *kota; compare Southern Sami gåetie. Whether and how the
Borrowed from Middle Low German lâke (“brine; standing water”), from Old Saxon *laca, from Proto-West Germanic *laku (“steam, pool”).

parole.significato: a long, thin strip (of wood (or metal or the like), to conceal a joint (or for isolation or decoration), like for examp…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lista, probably from Middle Low German lîste, from Old Saxon *līsta, from Proto-West Germanic *līstā, from Proto-Germanic *līstǭ. Cognate with Danish liste, Icelandic lista.

parole.significato: a plumb bob, a plummet, a weight (hanging)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lodh, from Middle Low German lot, from Old Saxon lōd, from Proto-West Germanic *laud.

parole.significato: a race (running competition or (in an extended sense) other speed competition, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lop, from Middle Low German lôp, from Old Saxon hlōpan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną. Related to the verb löpa, corresponding to German laufen and English leap.

parole.significato: to loosen ((from) something that binds or blocks, completely or partially)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lössa, from Middle Low German lossen, derived from the adjective los (“loose”), from Old Saxon lōs, from Proto-West Germanic *laus.
From Old Swedish langsamber, from Middle Low German lanksam, lanksum, from Old Saxon langsam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”). Equivalent to lång + -sam.
From Old Swedish makt, from Middle Low German macht, from Old Saxon maht, from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz. Compare mäktig.
From Middle Low German marschalk, from Old Saxon *marhskalk, from Proto-West Germanic *marhaskalk, from *marh (“horse”) + *skalk (“servant”).
From Middle Low German mast, from Old Saxon *mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast.

parole.significato: a tit (genus Parus), a small bird
parole.testo: From Middle Low German mêse, meise, from Old Saxon mēsa, from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ. Cognate to Norwegian Bokmål meis, meise and Norwegian Nynorsk meis, meise.
From Old Swedish morbär via dissimilation. Originally a borrowing of Middle Low German môrbēre, from Old Saxon *mōrberi, from Proto-West Germanic *mōrubaʀi.

parole.significato: A mosquito (small flying insect of the family Culicidae, known for biting and sucking blood).
parole.testo: From Middle Low German mügge, from Old Saxon muggia, from Proto-West Germanic *muggjā, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, *mujan, from Proto-Indo-European *mu (“fly”), *mew-. Cognates with Norwegian mygg, Icelandic mý, Danish myg, Old English myċġ, myċġe (whence Middle English migge, English midge); Old Hi

From Old Swedish mångel, from Middle Low German mangelen, from Old Saxon mangalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *mangalōn, from Latin mangō (“dealer, monger”). Attested since 1527. Cognate with Old Norse manga, Old English mangian, Middle High German mangâri.
From Old Swedish mat, from Middle Low German mât (modern Low German mâte, mât); ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *metan (“to measure”). Compare måtta.
Attested in Swedish at least since 1528; from Middle Low German narre, from Old Saxon *narro, from Proto-West Germanic *narrō. Cognate with Danish nar and Norwegian Nynorsk narr.
Borrowed from Middle Low German nēgede, from Old Saxon *nāhitha, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwiþu.
From Middle Low German nicken, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *hnīgan (“to bow”). Equivalent to nick + -a.

parole.significato: locality, place, location; a group of houses (of any size: hamlet, village, town, city...)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ort, from Old Saxon ord, from Proto-West Germanic *oʀd, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“sharp point, place”). Cognate with Middle English ord, North Frisian od (“tip, place, beginning”), Dutch oord (“place, region”), German Ort (“location, place, position”), Danish od (“a point”)
Inherited from Old Swedish pakke, from Middle Low German packe, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.
Derived from Middle Low German plicht, from Old Saxon *pliht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti.

parole.significato: to have a habit to do, to tend to do something
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plægha, from Middle Low German plegen, from Old Saxon plegan, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan.

parole.significato: a narrow, dark, passage between e.g. two buildings; a very narrow street
parole.testo: From Old Swedish prang, borrowed from Middle Low German prangen, from Old Saxon *prangan, from Proto-West Germanic *prangan (“to press”).

rams + lök. The first part is from Middle Low German ramese (“ramson”), from Old Saxon *hramuso, from Proto-West Germanic *hramusō. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk ramslauk and Danish ramsløg. Cognates amoung non-Scandinavian languages are Lithuanian kermùšė (and šermukšnis), Russian черемша (čeremša

parole.significato: an instance of traveling, "a travel"; a trip, a journey, a voyage, (in the plural) travels, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German reisen, from Old Saxon *reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.

Inherited from Old Swedish riddarliker, ridderligh, from Middle Low German ridderlik, from rider (“knight”, literally “rider”) + -līk (from Old Saxon -līk, from Proto-West Germanic *-līk). Analyzable as ryttare + -lig. Cognate of Dutch ridderlijk, German ritterlich.
From Old Swedish rokker, from Middle Low German rock, from Old Saxon rok, from Proto-West Germanic *(h)rokk, from Proto-Germanic *rukkaz.
Borrowed from Middle Low German roder, from Old Saxon *rōthar, from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr.
From Middle Low German rōf, from Old Saxon *rōf, from Proto-West Germanic *raub.
Borrowed from Middle Low German redik, from Old Saxon *rādik, from Proto-West Germanic *rādik, borrowed from Latin rādīcem. Doublet of radikal, rot, and rädisa.
From Middle Low German sä̂lich, older form of sêlich, from Old Saxon sālig, from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg.
From Old Swedish sinaper, sinapper, senaper, borrowed from Middle Low German senap, sennep, semp, from Proto-West Germanic *senap, from Latin sināpi.
From Old Swedish sinne, sin, from Middle Low German sin, from Old Saxon *sinn, from Proto-West Germanic *sinn.

parole.significato: to happen; in particular what happens during some extended period of time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ske, from Middle Low German schên, from Old Saxon skehan, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan. Cognate with Danish ske, Norwegian skje, German geschehen, Dutch geschieden, Limburgish sji-jje.

parole.significato: a rail (metal bar forming part of the track for a railroad)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skena, from Middle Low German schene, from Old Saxon scina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu, from Proto-Germanic *skinō. Influenced by German Schiene. First attested in 1478.
Inherited from Old Swedish skona, from Middle Low German schonen, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunōn.

parole.significato: to avoid (due to fear, disgust, or the like), to shun
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schǖwen, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhijan. Compare origin of skygg.

parole.significato: desecrate, defile, violate (treat (something ordinarily respected) with grave disrespect)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skænda, from Middle Low German schenden, from Old Saxon *skendian, from Proto-West Germanic *skandijan. Cognate of Danish skænde, Dutch schenden, German schänden, Old English scendan.
From Middle Low German scherm, from Old Saxon *skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi (“fur, pelt, covering, screen”).

parole.significato: a cabinet, a cupboard, a locker (either separate from, or built into, a wall, usually with shelves)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skap, from Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Cognate with Icelandic skápur.

From Old Swedish skön, from Middle Low German schö̂ne, from Old Saxon skōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz (“beautiful, shining”), related to *skuþōną, which yielded skåda (“to watch, to behold”). Compare German schön, English sheen, Danish skøn.

parole.significato: a slut, a floozy, a trollop (promiscuous woman)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish slinka, from Middle Low German slinken, from Old Saxon *slinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *slinkan, from Proto-Germanic *slinkaną. The noun is derived from the verb.
From Middle Low German slipen, from Proto-West Germanic *slīpan (“to grind, whet, sharpen”).

parole.significato: to drag (with difficulty) over a surface
parole.testo: From Old Swedish slēpa, from Middle Low German slēpen, from Old Saxon *slēpian, from Proto-West Germanic *slaipijan.
Inherited from Old Swedish smaker, from Middle Low German smak, smake, from Old Saxon *smakk, *smak, from Proto-West Germanic *smakku.

parole.significato: to taste (sample the flavor of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish smaka, from Middle Low German smaken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *smakōn, equivalent to smak + -a. Cognate with Danish smage, Middle English smaken.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smerten, from Old Saxon *smertan, from Proto-West Germanic *smertan.

parole.significato: to snore; to make noises while asleep
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German snorken, snarken, from Old Saxon *snarkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *snarkōn.
Originally meaning "snout," from Middle Low German snûte, from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt.

From Old Swedish speia, from Middle Low German spējen, from Old Saxon *spehōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną. Cognate of Danish speide, German spähen. Doublet of spå. See also origin for spion.

parole.significato: a play, a game; a person's or animal's happy, joyous movement or entertainment; activity for amusement only; a pursuit…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spil, from Middle Low German spil and Old Saxon spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil.

Old Swedish spill, from Middle Low German spille, from Old Saxon spinnila, from Proto-West Germanic *spinnilu, cognate with German Spindel and English spindle. With time, the Swedish word has adopted the declension pattern of spel in Etymology 1. Note that spindel is also a Swedish word.
Inherited from Old Swedish stikta, from Middle Low German stichten, from Proto-West Germanic *stiftijan conflated with *stihtijan.
From Middle Low German stille, from Old Saxon stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.

parole.significato: to stink, to reek (smell very bad)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stinka, from Middle Low German stinken, from Old Saxon stinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *stinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną. First attested in 1491. Cognate with Dutch and German stinken, Danish stinke, English stink.
From Middle Low German stȫven, from Old Saxon *stiovan, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan.

From Middle Low German straffen, from Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”). Compare with German Strafe. Etymologies 2, 3, and 4 below are all clippings of compounds from Etymology 1.

parole.significato: a short(ish) line; a line, a dash
parole.testo: Used in this form in the Bible translation of 1541. From Middle Low German streke, from Old Saxon *striki, from Proto-West Germanic *striki. Cognate with Norwegian strek, Danish streg, corresponding to Gothic striks, Middle Low German streke, Middle High German and German Strich, related to German v
From Middle Low German strunt, from Old Saxon *strunt, from Proto-West Germanic *strunt.

parole.significato: a ray, a beam (of light, radiation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German strâle, from Old Saxon strāla, from Proto-West Germanic *strālu (“beam”), also "arrow."

parole.significato: a voice (language; words; speech; expression; signification of feeling or opinion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stemmen, from Old Saxon *stemnian, from Proto-West Germanic *stabnijan, from Proto-Germanic *stabnijaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish sunder, from Middle Low German sunt, from Old Saxon *sund, from Proto-West Germanic *sund.

parole.significato: weak; lacking in force or ability
parole.testo: From Middle Low German swak, from Old Saxon *swak, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Compare with German schwach. The form with -g- is due to Danish influence.

parole.significato: to swing (move (something) in an arcing motion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German swingen, from Proto-West Germanic *swingan. Cognate of German schwingen, English swing. Doublet of svänga and schvung.

parole.significato: to cease, to vanish, to disappear, to diminish, to fade
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svinda, svinna, borrowed from Middle Low German swinden, from Old Saxon swindan, from Proto-West Germanic *swindan.
Borrowed from Middle Low German swengen, from Proto-West Germanic *swangijan. Cognate of Old English swenġan, Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐍃𐍅𐌰𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (afswaggwjan). Doublet of svinga.
From Middle Low German seker, from Old Saxon sikur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur, from Latin sēcūrus.
From Old Swedish talgher, from Middle Low German talch, from Old Saxon *talg, from Proto-West Germanic *talg, from Proto-Germanic *talgaz.

parole.significato: a tuft or lock of hair
parole.testo: From Old Swedish test, related to tesa (“to pull out wool”), from Middle Low German tēsen, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *taisan (“to pull apart, tug”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German trampen, from Old Saxon *trampan, from Proto-West Germanic *trampan (“to step”).

parole.significato: staircase, stairway, stairs, flight of stairs
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trapa, trappa, borrowed from Middle Low German trappe, from Old Saxon *trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā. Similar to Norwegian trapp, Danish trappe and Faroese trappa.
From Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.

parole.significato: to walk (in a somewhat slow and dignified manner, usually crossing some boundary); to step, to walk
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trædha, from Middle Low German treden, from Old Saxon *tredan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną. Doublet of tråda, from Old Norse.

From Old Swedish tvifla, borrowed from Middle Low German twīvel (“doubt”), from Old Saxon *twīfal, from Proto-West Germanic *twīfl. Related to Dutch twijfel, German Zweifel and the number two/zwei/två/tve.

parole.significato: tent; a pavilion or portable lodge
parole.testo: From Middle Low German telt, from *Old Saxon *teld, from Proto-West Germanic *teld, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Displaced Old Swedish tiæld, from Old Norse tjald, from the same Germanic source, compare tjäll.

parole.significato: a train (locomotive along with a line of coupled railroad cars pulled by it)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German toge, toch, from Old Saxon *tugi, from Proto-West Germanic *tugi. Cognate with Dutch teug, German Zug, Old English tyge. Swedes would make no difference between tåg in vikingatåg (“viking raid”), korståg (“crusade”), fälttåg, krigståg, and plundringståg (“pillage raid”), but i
Borrowed from Middle Low German wachtele, from Old Saxon *hwahtula, from Proto-West Germanic *hwahtlā.
From Old Swedish vandra, borrowed from Middle Low German wanderen, from Old Saxon *wandarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn.

parole.significato: to stroll, to wander, to walk without hurry
parole.testo: From Old Swedish vanka, probably borrowed from Middle Low German wanken, from Old Saxon wankon, from Proto-West Germanic *wankōn, from Proto-Germanic *wankōną, cognate with Danish vanke and Old Norse vakka.
From Middle Low German winkel, from Old Saxon *winkil, from Proto-West Germanic *winkil, from Proto-Indo-European *weng-.
From Middle Low German wōnunge, wāninge, from Old Saxon *wonunga, *wununga, from Proto-West Germanic *wunungu. Cognate with English woning, German Wohnung, Dutch woning.

parole.significato: genuine, authentic; not faked or counterfeit
parole.testo: From older spelling ekta, from Middle Low German echt, from Proto-West Germanic *aiwahaft. Cognate with Icelandic ekta, Norwegian Nynorsk ekte and Danish ægte.

Inherited from Old Swedish ämbar, from Middle Low German [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *ambrī, likely borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μφορεύς (ămphoreús). Doublet of amfora. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ambar and Riksmål Norwegian amber.
From Old Swedish ǣrlīker, from Middle Low German êrlich, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀulīk, equivalent to ära + -lig. Cognate of German ehrlich.

parole.significato: request (in particular a certain amount of money)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æskia (“to demand; to invite”), from Middle Low German eschen or Middle Low German eischen, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn. Cognate with English ask.
From Middle Low German even, effen, from Old Saxon evan, from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, cognate with English even, Dutch even. Compare Danish effen. See also jämn.

parole.significato: to translate; to change from one language to another, usually written text
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫversetten, ōversetten, from Old Saxon *ovarsettian, from Proto-West Germanic *ubarsattjan. Equivalent to över + sätta. Cognate with English overset, German übersetzen.
